title: POC EventBridge SDK & Function-calling Check-in
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on the EventBridge-based invocation pattern the customer is testing. Reviewed SDK shim behavior, function-calling reliability, schema for structured outputs, and latest latency/throughput numbers from the sandbox. Customer surfaced two blockers: intermittent serialization errors in the function payloads and KMS policy constraints for key rotation. Redwood agreed to share a sample SDK wrapper, small replay harness, and a short troubleshooting checklist. Next step: customer to run the replay test and upload logs; Redwood to deliver sample code and updated pricing addendum for burst capacity.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-18 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mike Thompson (BlueMesa Lead Eng), Sara Velez (PM), Dinesh Rao (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): short notes about EventBridge pattern checks, noted serialization flakiness and KMS questions.

Topics: SDK adapter, function calling reliability, structured output contract, latency numbers, KMS/audit logs

Action items (see metadata for owners/dates)

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh let’s do a quick roll call — Priya are you on?
[00:05] Priya: yep, hi all, Priya here, SE on the account. Jordan I think we said 45 minutes?
[00:09] Jordan: yeah 45 should be fine — uh I’ll kick things off then mike can do the run-through of the errors you saw.
[00:15] Mike: cool thanks, hey uh thanks Jordan, Priya, and Sara, Dinesh is on as well — big thanks for squeezing us in.
[00:20] Sara: hi, thanks — we have a packed list so wanna focus on two things: repro of the serialization error and the latency numbers from sandbox.
[00:27] Jordan: perfect. Priya do you wanna walk the SDK shim we shipped last week briefly? just to set the context.
[00:32] Priya: sure — so the shim is intentionally thin: it accepts an EventBridge event, normalizes headers, does a small sign check, then maps to the function-calling contract we discussed — basically functionName + args blob. It also attempts to validate the structured output JSON schema before returning. A few gotchas we found are around nested arrays and binary blobs — those need base64; sometimes the front-end was sending raw binary which caused the serializer to choke.
[01:05] Mike: yeah that lines up — our front-end was wrapping images inline, oops, that’s on us. The error we saw in prod-sim was something like "TypeError: Unexpected token in JSON at position 124" and then the function timed out, we saw some retries from EventBridge.
[01:20] Priya: mm-hmm the retry behavior is expected: EventBridge will retry on 5xx unless you set dlq. But the serializer error is 4xx-ish — it bubbles back. We also saw in the logs a couple of K V cache references but sometimes the name got munged to KBC — likely transcription or log parsing noise.
[01:38] Dinesh: on the security side we’re concerned about KMS key rotation — our policy rotates keys quarterly and the shim needs to work with our HSM/KMS flow. We need to ensure no cold-starts cause auth failures and that audit logs include token usage per invocation.
[01:50] Priya: understood — Redwood's private deployment supports customer-managed keys and HSM integrations, and we can show the audit log format — but we'll need your KMS policy excerpt to validate.
[02:00] Jordan: quick check — Mike, can you confirm the test traffic you're running is the week-of-replay you promised? we want to make sure the shim sees realistic event shapes.
[02:06] Mike: yes, we exported seven days of EventBridge events and will replay at 1x and 5x. The problem spikes at higher concurrency. at 5x we saw more failures.
[02:15] Priya: that's likely a backpressure / serialization race — if multiple workers are writing to the same temp buffer without locking you can have mangled JSON. In our sample shim we added a per-request buffer and thread-safe serializer.
[02:27] Sara: can you explain the structured output contract again? our product folks want to be sure the function returns stable keys.
[02:32] Priya: yeah so the contract is small: { status: string, result: {type: string, payload: object}, trace_id: string, meta: { model_version: string } } — we encourage avoiding arrays at the top level for deterministic parsing. Also, function-calling style responses should include explicit error codes not free-text error messages for easier routing.
[02:55] Mike: got it — we saw the function return sometimes a stringified JSON inside the payload which then got double-encoded. that was our bug but we need the shim to guard against that and emit a clear error.
[03:06] Priya: we can add a validation step that rejects double-encoded payloads and returns a clear 4xx with a code. we'll push that change to the sample repo.
[03:12] Jordan: great — now on latency numbers, Priya you ran the sandbox with the customer payloads right? any notable p50/p95?
[03:19] Priya: yes — with the current quantized runtime we saw p50 ~ 85ms, p95 around 420ms at 1x. at 5x concurrency p95 jumps to ~820ms in the sandbox with the current queueing config. Important note: the sandbox uses shared capacity so numbers vary; Dedicated or pinned pools will be flatter.
[03:39] Mike: okay 820ms is borderline for our UX flows — we target sub-500 for interactive parts. what's the easiest lever to get that down without dedicated right away?
[03:48] Priya: batching parameters and KV cache warmup help — if you pin a subset of hot prefixes we will serve from cache and cut p95 significantly. Also quantization profile can be tuned per workload; you might accept a tiny quality delta to gain latency. We can provide tuning recommendations.
[04:03] Sara: and cost tradeoffs? if we warm caches aggressively what's the billing impact?
[04:07] Jordan: warming cache increases token compute time but reduces repeated compute; net effect depends on request duplication. For your distribution with many repeated prompts, caching will lower unit cost. we'll send an estimated workbook.
[04:16] Dinesh: on compliance — we need audit logs showing request id, model_version, invoking principal, and KMS key version. can Redwood provide those fields?
[04:24] Priya: yes, we capture trace_id, model_version, and principal. KMS key id is surfaced in the audit record for private deployments. For hosted we can do partial — but for enterprise private we can guarantee full KMS linkage.
[04:35] Mike: another small issue — function timeouts: some functions are set to 2s and our model responses hit that at 5x concurrency. is there a recommended timeout to set?
[04:43] Priya: we'd recommend 8-10s for heavier responses with streaming; for short lookups 2-3s is fine. But it's workload dependent — we'll provide a short guidance doc.
[04:51] Jordan: quick question on observability — are the token-level costs visible per-route in the console?
[04:56] Priya: yes per-route breakdown, plus per-token breakdown in the telemetry. we can add a temporary dashboard and grant BlueMesa access to your trial tenant.
[05:05] Mike: excellent — thanks. Anything else on the technical side?
[05:09] Sara: just one ask — can the shim emit a well-defined error message for double-encoded payloads and include the offending trace_id so we can correlate logs?
[05:16] Priya: yes will do. Also will include a small unit test in the sample repo that demonstrates the double-encoding detection.
[05:23] Jordan: ok let's move to blockers and next steps then. Dinesh can you summarize KMS asks?
[05:28] Dinesh: we need: 1) confirmation on key rotation handling to ensure no dropouts; 2) confirm where audit logs are stored and retention; 3) a statement about HSM support for private deployments.
[05:38] Priya: we can provide an integration note covering 1 and 3, and an audit-log sample for 2.
[05:43] Jordan: perfect. Action items are captured — quick recap: Redwood to share sample SDK repo + replay harness (Priya) — BlueMesa to run replay and upload logs (Mike) — Jordan to send pricing addendum — Dinesh to send KMS policy.
[05:58] Mike: timeline check — we can do the run this week and have results by Friday.
[06:02] Jordan: great, we'll aim to have the sample up by Tuesday EOD.
[06:07] Sara: do we want a follow-up deep dive on KMS? tentatively suggest 06/29.
[06:12] Dinesh: 06/29 works.
[06:15] Priya: okay I'll pencil it in and prepare the integration doc.
[06:19] Jordan: cool. any competitors that you considered while doing this POC? Mike, Sara?
[06:24] Mike: we looked at AWS Lambda + EventBridge but they lack the same quantization/throughput tooling; also briefly evaluated Anthropic for model outputs but they didn't meet cost targets.
[06:34] Jordan: okay good to know.
[06:36] Sara: one last question — is there a recommended way to handle partial failures so we can surface best-effort results instead of full failure?
[06:44] Priya: yes, implement a partial result schema: status = partial, results = [successful, failed], and route failed ones to dlq for reprocessing. We'll add an example in the sample repo.
[06:56] Jordan: awesome. If no other items, we'll close and I will follow up with the deliverables.
[07:00] Mike: that's it thanks everyone.
[07:03] Jordan: thanks — meeting adjourned.

Notes about transcript quality: occasional mis-attribution and log parser noise (e.g., KVC/KBC vs KV cache). Some technical terms spelled out by speaker (SAML as s a m l). There were short overlapping talk turns near the end.
